questions.q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
questions.why: A vector has size and direction; velocity is speed in a stated direction.

questions.q: A stopwatch times 20 swings of a pendulum as 30.0 s. What is the period of one swing?
questions.why: Period = total time ÷ number of swings = 30.0 ÷ 20 = 1.5 s. Timing many swings reduces the reaction-time error.

questions.q: What does a micrometer screw gauge measure best?
o: The diameter of a thin wire
questions.why: It measures small lengths, such as a wire's diameter, to about 0.01 mm.

questions.q: Which is a scalar quantity?
questions.why: Temperature has size only, no direction.

questions.q: A car travels 120 m in 8.0 s at constant speed. What is its speed?
questions.why: Speed = distance ÷ time = 120 ÷ 8.0 = 15 m/s.

questions.q: On a speed–time graph, what does the area under the line give?
questions.why: Area under a speed–time graph = speed × time = distance travelled.

questions.q: A cyclist speeds up from 2 m/s to 8 m/s in 3 s. What is the acceleration?
questions.why: a = change in velocity ÷ time = (8 − 2) ÷ 3 = 2 m/s².

questions.q: A distance–time graph is a straight sloping line. What does this show?
questions.why: A constant gradient on a distance–time graph means constant speed.

questions.q: Near the Earth's surface and without air resistance, a falling object accelerates at about…
questions.why: The acceleration of free fall, g, is about 9.8 m/s².

questions.q: A space station orbits at 6800 km from the centre of the Earth. How far does it travel in one orbit?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates used the radius as the distance. One orbit is the circumference 2πr = 2π × 6800 ≈ 42 700 km.

long.q: A car accelerates uniformly from 5.0 m/s to 25 m/s in 8.0 s. Calculate its acceleration and the distance it travels in this time.

questions.q: What is the weight of a 5.0 kg mass where g = 9.8 N/kg?
An astronaut goes from the Earth to the Moon. What happens?
questions.why: Mass is the amount of matter and doesn't change; weight depends on the gravitational field strength, which is weaker on the Moon.

questions.q: Weight is measured in…
questions.why: Weight is a force, so its unit is the newton.

questions.q: A block has mass 600 g and volume 200 cm³. What is its density?
questions.why: Density = mass ÷ volume = 600 ÷ 200 = 3.0 g/cm³.

questions.q: An object floats in water. What can you say about its density?
questions.why: Objects less dense than the liquid float in it.

questions.q: How do you find the volume of an irregular stone?
o: Lower it into a measuring cylinder of water and read the rise
questions.why: The volume of water displaced equals the stone's volume.

long.q: A stone of mass 240 g is lowered into a measuring cylinder. The water level rises from 50 cm³ to 146 cm³. Calculate the density of the stone.

questions.q: A resultant force of 12 N acts on a 3.0 kg mass. What is its acceleration?
A spring stretches 2.0 cm with a 4.0 N load. Within its limit of proportionality, what load stretches it 5.0 cm?
questions.why: Extension is proportional to load: k = 4.0 ÷ 2.0 = 2.0 N/cm, so 5.0 cm needs 10 N.

questions.q: A skydiver falls at terminal velocity. Which is true?
o: Weight is greater than air resistance
Air resistance is greater than weight
questions.why: At terminal velocity the forces balance, so there is no resultant force and no acceleration.

questions.q: A 4 N force acts 0.5 m from a pivot. What is the moment?
questions.why: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot = 4 × 0.5 = 2 N m.

questions.q: What keeps an object moving in a circle at constant speed?
o: A force along its direction of motion
A force away from the centre
questions.why: A force perpendicular to the motion, towards the centre, changes the direction but not the speed.

questions.q: A cyclist travels at a constant speed along a straight, level road. Which statement is correct?
o: The driving force is greater than the resistive forces
The driving force equals the resistive forces
There is no friction at all
Friction is smaller than the driving force but not zero
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a popular wrong answer said friction must be less than the driving force. Constant velocity means the resultant force is zero.

questions.q: What is the momentum of a 2.0 kg ball moving at 3.0 m/s?
In a collision with no external forces, what is conserved?
questions.why: Total momentum is always conserved when no external force acts.

questions.q: Impulse is equal to…
questions.why: Impulse = FΔt, which equals the change in momentum.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg ball moves at 3.0 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
A 50 kg student climbs 4.0 m. What is the gain in gravitational potential energy? (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A motor does 600 J of work in 12 s. What is its power?
questions.why: Power = work done ÷ time = 600 ÷ 12 = 50 W.

questions.q: A lamp takes in 100 J and gives out 20 J as light. What is its efficiency?
questions.why: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input × 100% = 20 ÷ 100 = 20%.

questions.q: Which energy resource is renewable?
questions.why: Geothermal energy comes from heat inside the Earth and is not used up.

questions.q: Wind passes through a wind turbine and the blades turn. What happens to the air?
o: It speeds up and gains kinetic energy
It slows down because some of its kinetic energy is transferred to the turbine
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many thought the air speeds up. Energy taken by the turbine comes from the air's kinetic energy, so the air slows.

long.q: A student of mass 60 kg climbs a flight of stairs 3.0 m high in 4.0 s. Calculate the useful power developed. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

questions.q: A 600 N force acts on 0.20 m². What is the pressure?
Why do snowshoes stop you sinking into snow?
o: They spread your weight over a larger area, reducing pressure
questions.why: Same force over a larger area gives a smaller pressure.

questions.q: What is the pressure due to 10 m of water? (density 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg)

long.q: Calculate the pressure due to the water at a depth of 12 m. (Density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg)

questions.q: In which state are particles close together but able to move past each other?
questions.why: Liquid particles touch but can slide past one another.

questions.q: Gas in a sealed container is heated. Why does its pressure rise?
o: The particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often
questions.why: Higher temperature means faster particles, so more frequent and harder collisions with the walls.

questions.q: A gas at constant temperature is squashed to half its volume. Its pressure…
questions.why: At constant temperature pV is constant, so halving V doubles p.

questions.q: What is absolute zero?
questions.why: −273 °C (0 K) is the temperature at which particles have the least possible kinetic energy.

questions.q: Why does evaporation cool the liquid left behind?
o: The fastest particles escape, lowering the average energy of those left
questions.why: The most energetic particles leave the surface, so the average kinetic energy, and the temperature, of the rest falls.

questions.q: Which describes the particles in a liquid?
o: They are close together and move randomly
They are far apart and move at high speed
They do not move at all
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some said particles in a liquid vibrate about fixed points; that describes a solid.

questions.q: Why are gaps left between sections of railway track?
o: To allow for thermal expansion in hot weather
questions.why: Steel expands when heated; the gaps stop the rails buckling.

questions.q: How much energy raises 2.0 kg of water by 5.0 °C? (c = 4200 J/(kg °C))
While ice melts at 0 °C, its temperature…
questions.why: Energy goes into breaking the forces between particles, not raising the temperature.

questions.q: What is true of the particles of a substance at absolute zero?
o: They have the least gravitational potential energy
They have the least possible kinetic energy
They move faster than at any other temperature
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a common misconception linked absolute zero to gravitational potential energy. It is the temperature of least kinetic energy.

long.q: Calculate the energy needed to heat 0.50 kg of water from 20 °C to 80 °C. (Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg °C))

questions.q: How does thermal energy reach the Earth from the Sun?
questions.why: Space is a vacuum, so only radiation can carry energy across it.

questions.q: Which surface is the best emitter of infrared radiation?
questions.why: Dull black surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers of infrared.

questions.q: Why is the heating element at the bottom of a kettle?
o: Hot water rises, setting up convection currents
questions.why: Heated water expands, becomes less dense and rises; cooler water sinks to be heated.

questions.q: Why is a metal spoon a better conductor than a plastic one?
o: It has free electrons that carry energy
questions.why: Metals conduct well because delocalised electrons transfer energy quickly.

questions.q: Which outside surface keeps hot coffee in a cup warm for the longest?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many chose black. Shiny, light surfaces are poor emitters of infrared, so less thermal energy is lost.

questions.q: A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4.0 m. What is its speed?
Which wave is longitudinal?
questions.why: In sound the vibrations are parallel to the direction the wave travels.

questions.q: Water waves pass from deep to shallow water. What happens?
o: They slow down and their wavelength shortens
questions.why: Waves slow in shallow water; frequency stays the same, so wavelength decreases (refraction).

questions.q: Diffraction through a gap is greatest when the gap is…
o: about the same size as the wavelength
much smaller than the wave's amplitude
questions.why: Spreading is greatest when the gap width is similar to the wavelength.

questions.q: Which statement about water waves in a ripple tank is correct?
o: They carry water from one end of the tank to the other
questions.why: Examiners (2023): most candidates said water waves are longitudinal. The water moves up and down, at right angles to the direction the wave travels.

questions.q: A ray hits a plane mirror at 30° to the normal. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.why: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured from the normal.

questions.q: Light enters glass at 40° to the normal and refracts to 25°. What is the refractive index? (sin 40° = 0.643, sin 25° = 0.423)
Total internal reflection can happen when light…
o: goes from glass into air at more than the critical angle
goes from glass into air at less than the critical angle
questions.why: It needs light travelling into a less dense medium at an angle bigger than the critical angle.

questions.q: What kind of image does a converging lens make of a distant object on a screen?
questions.why: An image you can catch on a screen is real; for a distant object it is inverted and diminished.

long.q: Light passes from air into glass. The angle of incidence is 40° and the angle of refraction is 25°. Calculate the refractive index of the glass.
scheme: C1: n = sin i ÷ sin r

questions.q: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum has the shortest wavelength?
questions.why: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and highest frequency.

questions.q: All electromagnetic waves travel in a vacuum at…
questions.why: All EM waves travel at the speed of light, 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, in a vacuum.

questions.q: Which is used in TV remote controls?
questions.why: Remote controls send short-range infrared signals.

questions.q: Which can damage skin cells and cause skin cancer?
questions.why: Ultraviolet radiation can damage cells in the skin.

questions.q: Which region of the electromagnetic spectrum is used for satellite television?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): infrared was a common wrong choice. Microwaves pass through the atmosphere to and from satellites.

questions.q: Which describes a digital signal?
o: A series of pulses with only two values, such as 1 and 0
A signal that can only travel through optical fibres
A signal that cannot be regenerated
questions.why: Examiners (2023): weaker candidates described digital signals as continuous. That is an analogue signal.

questions.q: What is the range of human hearing?
questions.why: Healthy young people hear roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

questions.q: Why can't sound travel through space?
o: There are no particles to vibrate
questions.why: Sound needs a medium; a vacuum has no particles to pass on the vibrations.

questions.q: An echo returns 2.0 s after a shout towards a cliff. Sound travels at 340 m/s. How far away is the cliff?
questions.why: The sound travels there and back: distance = (340 × 2.0) ÷ 2 = 340 m.

questions.q: A louder sound has a larger…
questions.why: Loudness depends on amplitude; pitch depends on frequency.

questions.q: Which material is magnetically soft, used in electromagnet cores?
questions.why: Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily.

questions.q: What happens when two north poles are brought together?
questions.why: Like poles repel.

questions.q: Field lines around a bar magnet point…
o: from south to north outside the magnet
from north to south outside the magnet
questions.why: By convention, field lines go from north to south outside a magnet.

questions.q: A current of 2.0 A flows for 30 s. How much charge passes?
A resistor has 6.0 V across it and 0.50 A through it. What is its resistance?
A 2.0 kW heater runs for 3.0 hours. How much energy does it use?
How does the resistance of a wire change if its length doubles?
questions.why: Resistance is proportional to length.

questions.q: The resistance of a thermistor as it gets hotter…
questions.why: An NTC thermistor's resistance falls as temperature rises.

questions.q: A current of 0.50 A flows through a lamp for 1 minute. How much charge passes through the lamp?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): the most common error was not converting 1 minute to 60 s in Q = It. Q = 0.50 × 60 = 30 C.

questions.q: A wire is replaced by one of the same material and length but twice the diameter. What happens to its resistance?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some thought resistance is inversely proportional to diameter. R ∝ 1/area and area ∝ diameter², so doubling the diameter quarters R.

questions.q: A plastic rod becomes positively charged when rubbed with a cloth. Why?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some thought gaining electrons makes a rod positive. Only electrons move; losing negative charge leaves the rod positive.

questions.q: Resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are in series. What is the total resistance?
questions.why: In series, resistances add: 4 + 6 = 10 Ω.

questions.q: Two 6 Ω resistors are in parallel. What is the combined resistance?
questions.why: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3, so R = 3 Ω. Parallel is always less than the smallest branch.

questions.q: In a parallel circuit, what is the same across each branch?
questions.why: Each branch is connected across the same two points, so has the same p.d.

questions.q: A light-dependent resistor's resistance in bright light is…
questions.why: An LDR's resistance falls as light intensity increases.

long.q: Resistors of 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω are connected in parallel to a 6.0 V supply. Calculate the combined resistance and the current from the supply.

questions.q: What does a fuse do?
o: Melts and breaks the circuit if the current is too large
questions.why: It protects the cable from overheating by breaking the circuit when the current is too high.

questions.q: A kettle uses 2300 W on 230 V. Which fuse fits best?
questions.why: I = P ÷ V = 10 A, so use the next fuse rating above: 13 A.

questions.q: Why is a metal-cased appliance earthed?
o: So a fault sends a large current to earth and blows the fuse
questions.why: If the live wire touches the case, current flows to earth, the fuse blows and the case can't stay live.

questions.q: In a correctly wired mains plug and appliance, where are the fuse and the switch connected?
o: Switch in the neutral wire, fuse in the earth wire
Switch in the live wire, fuse in the earth wire
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some put them in the neutral or earth wire. Both go in the live wire so the appliance is isolated from the high voltage.

questions.q: A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a meter. What happens?
o: An e.m.f. is induced while the magnet moves
A current flows only when the magnet is still
The coil becomes a permanent magnet
questions.why: A changing magnetic field through the coil induces an e.m.f.; no movement, no induced e.m.f.

questions.q: A transformer has 100 turns on the primary and 500 on the secondary. Input is 12 V a.c. What is the output?
questions.why: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, so Vs = 12 × 500 ÷ 100 = 60 V (a step-up transformer).

questions.q: Why is electricity transmitted at very high voltage?
o: The current is smaller, so less energy is lost as heat in the cables
questions.why: For the same power, higher voltage means lower current, and cable losses depend on I²R.

questions.q: What does the split-ring commutator do in a d.c. motor?
o: Reverses the current in the coil every half turn
questions.why: Reversing the current each half turn keeps the coil turning the same way.

questions.q: A bar magnet is moved into a coil connected to a voltmeter. Which change gives the largest induced e.m.f.?
o: Moving the magnet in more slowly
Holding the magnet still inside the coil
Using a coil with fewer turns
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many thought slow movement induces more. The e.m.f. depends on how fast the magnetic field through the coil changes.

questions.q: Which statement about a step-up transformer is correct?
o: The primary coil has more turns than the secondary
The secondary coil has more turns than the primary
An alternating current flows in the iron core
It works with a steady direct current
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates mixed up the coils and thought current flows in the core. Step-up means Ns > Np; the core carries a changing magnetic field.

topics.name: The nuclear model of the atom

questions.q: A nucleus of carbon-14 has 6 protons. How many neutrons?
questions.why: Neutrons = nucleon number − proton number = 14 − 6 = 8.

questions.q: Isotopes of an element have the same number of…
questions.why: Isotopes have the same proton number but different numbers of neutrons.

questions.q: What did the alpha-scattering experiment show?
o: Most of an atom is empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus
questions.why: Most alpha particles passed straight through; a few bounced back from a small, dense, positive centre.

questions.q: Which radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?
questions.why: Alpha particles are large and highly ionising, so they are stopped by paper or a few cm of air.

questions.q: A sample has a half-life of 3 days. What fraction is left after 9 days?
questions.why: 9 days is 3 half-lives: ½ × ½ × ½ = 1/8.

questions.q: What is emitted in beta decay?
o: A fast-moving electron from the nucleus
questions.why: A neutron changes into a proton and a fast electron (beta particle) leaves the nucleus.

questions.q: Which is the most penetrating radiation?
questions.why: Gamma is only reduced by thick lead or concrete.

questions.q: A counter reads 260 counts per minute near a source. The background count rate is 20 counts per minute. What is the count rate due to the source?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): weaker candidates forgot to subtract background, others added it. Source rate = measured − background.

long.q: A radioactive source has a half-life of 6 hours and an activity of 800 Bq. Calculate its activity after 24 hours.

questions.q: What causes day and night on Earth?
o: The Earth spinning on its axis
questions.why: One rotation of the Earth on its axis takes about 24 hours.

questions.q: What causes the seasons?
o: The Earth's changing distance from the Sun
The tilt of the Earth's axis
questions.why: The tilted axis means each hemisphere gets more direct sunlight for part of the year.

questions.q: Light from the Sun takes about 500 s to reach Earth. Light travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. How far is the Sun?
questions.why: distance = speed × time = 3.0 × 10⁸ × 500 = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m.

questions.q: How many stars are there in our Solar System?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some weaker candidates thought there are many. The Sun is the only star; the others are in our galaxy, not the Solar System.

questions.q: What is a light-year?
o: The distance light travels in one year
The time for light to reach the Moon
questions.why: It is a distance: about 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m.

questions.q: What is the evidence that the Universe is expanding?
o: Light from distant galaxies is redshifted
questions.why: Redshift shows galaxies moving away; the further away, the faster (and greater the redshift).

questions.q: What keeps a main-sequence star stable?
o: A balance between gravity inwards and pressure from fusion outwards
questions.why: Inward gravitational force is balanced by outward pressure from the energy released by fusion.

questions.q: What will a star like the Sun become at the end of its life?
o: A white dwarf (after a red giant)
questions.why: A low-mass star swells into a red giant, then its core is left as a white dwarf.

questions.q: Which sequence is correct for a star with about the same mass as the Sun?
o: Protostar → stable star → red giant → planetary nebula and white dwarf
Red giant → protostar → stable star → white dwarf
Protostar → red supergiant → supernova → black hole
White dwarf → red giant → stable star → protostar
questions.why: Examiners (2023): this recall question (syllabus 6.2.2) was mostly well answered; supernovae and black holes are for much more massive stars.
